summary: This standards-track document defines how to map body parts of X.400 messages into MIME entities and back, including multipart and forwarded messages.

eli5.summary: Moving each item from one kind of package into another kind without losing anything.

subtitle: Rules for turning the parts of an X.400 message into MIME parts, and back, at a mail gateway.

tldr.problem: Gateways between X.400 mail and Internet MIME mail need to convert message bodies, including multipart and forwarded messages, and the two worlds carry non-text content in different ways.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines mappings between X.400 body parts and MIME content types, a set of encapsulations for content that cannot be mapped, optional headers that let a sender steer the gateway, and a registry of equivalences.
tldr.outcome: A conformant gateway can pass text, attachments, forwarded messages and multiparts across, and can wrap anything else so that a gateway on the far side can restore it without loss.

facts.label: Multiple body parts become
facts.value: multipart/mixed, or multipart/digest if all are messages

today: RFC 2157 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this unit lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Scope and Vocabulary
sections.content:
RFC 2157 is a companion to MIXER (RFC 1327), which defines the principles and the translation of headers for interworking between MIME-based RFC 822 mail and X.400 mail. This document defines how to map the body parts of X.400 messages into MIME entities and the reverse, including multipart and forwarded messages.

It uses a few terms precisely. An equivalence is a pair of mappings that together convert between an X.400 body part and a MIME body part without loss. Encapsulation wraps something from one mail system so the other can carry it, and a gateway going back the other way can always restore the original. Tunneling is what happens when one gateway encapsulates a message and another decapsulates it. Capitalized MUST, SHOULD and MAY follow RFC 2119.
sections.eli5: Two post offices use different kinds of envelopes. This paper explains how to move a letter's contents from one kind of envelope to the other, and what to do when something will not fit.

sections.title: Basic Conversion Rules
sections.content:
Going from MIME to X.400, a message with no MIME-Version header becomes a single IA5 text body part. If the header is present, the body is converted using whatever mappings the gateway has configured and implemented.

Going from X.400 to MIME, if the first body part is IA5 text starting with the line RFC-822-Headers:, the rest of that part is appended to the RFC 822 header. A single remaining IA5 body part whose first line is MIME-Version: 1.0 is taken to be a HARPOON-encapsulated body part. Any other IA5 text is mapped directly with the default 7bit encoding, and Quoted-Printable SHOULD be used if there are very long lines or non-ASCII or control characters.

If there are several body parts, the result is a MIME multipart. It is multipart/digest if all the parts are messages, and multipart/mixed otherwise, in the original order.

The RFC gives gateways wide latitude. A gateway may use what it knows about the recipient, a request from the sender, heuristics such as filenames, or the limits of the next hop. Where no mapping is known it may drop the part, reject the message or encapsulate it, and a conformant gateway MUST be configurable for encapsulation. Two gateways may therefore behave differently.
sections.eli5: Plain letters are copied across as they are. A bundle of several items becomes a folder with the items in the same order. Anything the gateway does not understand gets boxed up rather than thrown away, if it is set that way.

sections.title: Mapping File Transfer Body Part Parameters
sections.content:
New mappings are expected to carry content in the File Transfer Body Part (FTBP), using the profile defined by the EMA. This section fixes how the special FTBP parameters correspond to MIME headers in both directions.

  • Content-ID is encoded as an IPM message identifier in the related-stored-file field, and the relationship is set to the string Internet MIME Body Part.
  • Content-Description maps to the first string in the environment user-visible-string.
  • The filename of Content-Disposition maps to the FTBP pathname. The disposition itself is ignored going to X.400 and is always attachment coming back.
  • The creation, modification and read dates and the size map to the matching file attributes. Dates use the RFC 822 date format.
  • Other RFC 822 headers go into the FTBP extensions.

Some parameters are ASN.1 GraphicStrings, which can hold any registered character set. A gateway may either use the RFC 2047 encoded-word mechanism, or apply the normalization in Appendix A and replace non-ASCII characters with a question mark. Simply bit-stripping the result is NOT valid.

Filenames from the wire carry a warning. No special meaning is given to / and \, and normal security precautions MUST be taken before using one on a local file system.
sections.eli5: The little label on each attachment, like its name, date and size, is copied carefully from one kind of label to the other so nothing important is lost.

sections.title: Encapsulation Methods
sections.content:
When no mapping exists, the gateway can drop the part and leave a marker, reject the message, or encapsulate. The choice should be configurable. The RFC defines four ways to carry MIME inside X.400:

  • FTBP: undo the content-transfer-encoding and place the octets in the file transfer data, with all headers in the FTBP extensions. This is lossless, and counts as no conversion. It does not work for multiparts, which must first be mapped to a ForwardedIPMessage.
  • BP15: an extended body part with MimeParameters holding the content type, its parameters and the other header fields, and the body in canonical form as an octet string. It is compatible with RFC 1494.
  • IA5 (HARPOON): an IA5 text body part that begins with MIME-version: and then the Content-type and Content-transfer-encoding headers and the encoded content, as in RFC 1496. It preserves everything but the RFC calls it rather unhelpful for X.400 users.
  • BP14: strips all headers and undoes the transfer encoding to make a bilaterally defined body part. It is lossy and no reverse translation is defined.

In the other direction, any X.400 body part can travel as the MIME type application/x400-bp with a bp-type parameter, carrying the BER encoding of the body part. An FTBP body part that meets some conditions can instead be carried as application/x-ftbp. followed by the numbers of its object identifier.
sections.eli5: There are four ways to seal a parcel for the other post office. Some keep every detail so it can be opened exactly as it was. One just keeps the contents and throws the wrapping away.

sections.title: User Control Over the Gateway
sections.content:
A sender who knows more about the recipient than the gateway does can ask for a particular conversion. These headers override any conversion prohibited and conversion with loss prohibited settings. The mechanism is not part of the minimum conformance, but if it is implemented it should be done as described.

From MIME to X.400, the header is Wanted-X400-Conversion, with an optional from MIME type, an optional to object identifier or tunnel, and a required encoding of bp14, bp15, ftbp or ia5. If the target is omitted, tunnel is assumed. It can sit in the heading of a single body part, or in a multipart, where from is mandatory and the request applies to all matching parts, including nested ones, unless a part has its own header.

From X.400 to MIME, a wanted-MIME-conversion heading extension lists pairs of an X.400 body part type and the MIME type, with optional encoding and parameters, to use. If the gateway has no relevant mapping it proceeds as if the field were absent.
sections.eli5: The sender can write a note on the parcel saying how it should be repacked, if the sender knows something the post office does not.

sections.title: Equivalences and the Registry
sections.content:
An equivalence names a MIME type and an X.400 body part (often BP15 or FTAM) and must say enough to allow independent implementation, including the effect of conversion prohibited. Anyone can register one with IANA, but gateways need not support every registered one. The IESG can lock a registration, and all equivalences defined in standards-track documents, including this one, are locked.

The core equivalences are:

  • IA5Text and text/plain with US-ASCII, with no conversion. The IA5 currency symbol in position 2/4 is converted to the dollar symbol.
  • GeneralText and text/plain with ISO-8859-1 through ISO-8859-9 or iso-2022-jp, using a table of ISO registry numbers. The text must be normalized to remove escape and shift sequences, and Appendix A gives pseudocode.
  • BilaterallyDefined and the FTBP unknown attachment, both with application/octet-stream. Use of BilaterallyDefined is deprecated in X.400 but kept for backward compatibility with 1984 systems.
  • MessageBodyPart and message/RFC822 or multipart/*. For nested multiparts the gateway generates a heading whose subject depends on the subtype, for example Multipart Message for mixed.
  • Teletex and text/plain with charset Teletex, where pages are joined with a form feed.

Extended body parts must follow X.420: each is identified by object identifiers and defined with the EXTENDED-BODY-PART-TYPE macro, rooted at the MIXER mixer identifier. Other equivalences, for PostScript, images and ODA, are defined in RFC 2160, RFC 2158 and RFC 2161.
sections.eli5: The paper keeps a matching list: this kind of X.400 item pairs with that kind of Internet item. Anyone can suggest a new pair for the list.

sections.title: Conformance
sections.content:
To call itself MIXER conformant for body parts, a gateway must implement:

  • encapsulation of MIME in the FTBP body part, of X.400 body parts in x400-bp, and of FTBP body parts in application/x-ftbp.oid;
  • HARPOON encapsulation of security multiparts;
  • the mappings text/plain to IA5Text, text/plain with iso-8859-* to GeneralText, multipart/* and message/RFC822 to ForwardedIPMessage, and application/octet-stream to both FTBP unknown and BilaterallyDefined;
  • a configuration choice of which application/octet-stream translation to use.

Everything else MAY be implemented, but anything implemented MUST follow this specification. Several MIME types are listed as having special handling: message/external-body, message/partial, multipart/signed and multipart/encrypted. Gateways MUST support encapsulating each of them, and the signed and encrypted types by HARPOON.
sections.eli5: There is a checklist of jobs every gateway must be able to do, and anything extra it does must follow the same rules.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC names these issues: using filenames that arrive in body part headers, and letting a gateway handle encrypted or signed content. A gateway that fetches a message/external-body on the recipient's behalf may be tricked by malicious senders into performing inappropriate actions. The usual caveats about content that may contain executable code apply to user agents on both sides.

For multipart/signed, stripping the signature, re-signing with X.400 security, or other processing all break end-to-end security, and the recipient can trust the message no more than the gateway. Encapsulation is the only approach that keeps it, and it must use HARPOON because the signature is computed on the encoded body part. For multipart/encrypted the valid options are to decrypt, encapsulate or drop, but the RFC warns of grave security concerns about decrypting and says the MIXER working group strongly preferred encapsulation.
sections.eli5: A gateway that opens a sealed or signed letter can no longer promise nobody tampered with it. The safest choice is to pass the sealed letter along unopened.
